instructions: Rewrite `callout.text` per beat: 2-4 words, concrete and loaded, in the viewer's second person where it fits.
NEVER an abstract noun (ORGANIZATION / MANAGEMENT / INFORMATION). Prefer what a person can see, feel or do.
Set callout to null when the beat has no hook worth stamping — silence is a valid, good choice.
`style`: reveal (3-4 words) | highlight (2 words) | strike (a negation) | outline (a real stat) | box | stack.
`concept`: the beat's LITERAL subject → a scene icon that gets shown instead of talking heads.

Allowed: alarmClock, butterfly, subway, car, coffee, codeWindow, rocketLaunch, funnelMetrics, dollarExchange, laptopMockup, crash, ledge, water, grave, medical, notes, phone, school, home, family, road, storm, star, heart, fire, tree, mask, mirror, key, law, photo, war, game, work, city, food, coin, door, lightbulb, shadowSelf, puppeteer, chains, compass, dominoCascade, icebergDepth, funnelTrap, thirtyTyrants, ringOfGyges, caveAllegory, shipOfState, tripartiteSoul, kallipolis, fiveRegimes, mythOfEr, boulder, summit, ladder, crack, clock, balance, book, shield, trophy, hourglass, sword, target, magnifier, wallet, gift, inheritance, zap. Set a string when the beat is really ABOUT that thing
(a crash, a home, a lake, a wall of notes); null or omitted = no icon (there is no lexicon
fallback). Use only when it's the true subject — a wrong icon is worse than none. The icon must
be in the book's story-bible visualProvenance.allowedMotifs or it is dropped with a warning.
`set` (optional): the location, one of the renderer's sets — honoured as written.
`shotOverride` (optional): force a framing. `shot` above is only the director's first guess.
The director stages the body itself from the concept — a beat whose subject is a
letter/phone/key/photo/book/coin/mirror/mask/idea/compass/meal/love/job/court puts that
object IN THE LEAD'S HAND, an outdoor beat can make them walk across the set, an indoor
one can sit them down. You do not author that here; naming the right `concept` is what
turns it on. A wrong concept costs more now than it used to.
`diagram`: an EXPLANATORY self-drawing graphic that BECOMES the whole beat (cast dropped,
no callout). Author one ONLY on a genuinely conceptual beat; leave null otherwise — a weak
or generic diagram is worse than none. Use at most a handful across the whole book. Shape:
{ type, title?, labels[], values[] }, where type is one of:
sorter   — a taxonomy sorting into buckets. labels = the 2-4 category names; values = optional per-bucket counts.
matchWave— two rhythms drifting then locking into sync. labels[0] = the payoff word (e.g. IN SYNC).
flow     — a cause→effect chain. labels = 2-3 ordered node names.
spectrum — a marker on a continuum. labels = [leftPole, rightPole]; values = [0..1 marker position].
Keep labels 1-2 words. Best on the beat that first NAMES a framework, a sync, a process or a scale.

`concept: null` means NO icon on this beat (not even a decorative one); omitting the key is ALSO no icon — there is no lexicon fallback (Faz 0). Every beat needs an entry; an unauthored beat fails gate-authorship.
Do not leave a beat silent when its narration names concrete things (a list of objects, an anecdote, a person doing something) — give it the narrator's phrase or the object.
Prefer the narrator's concrete phrase over an abstract metaphor label ("PAUSE THE IMPULSE", not "A LOGIC FILTER").
A diagram title must not promise a shape its type cannot draw (no "LOOP"/"PYRAMID" on a straight flow).
Keep the array order and length. Then re-run plan-antidote with --callouts=<this file>.
After re-running: node scripts/audit-antidote.js --slug=<slug> — it FAILS the plan if any
window runs longer than 8s with nothing happening on screen.

beats.narration: You know, because when you really step back and like look at the architecture of the story, you realize August Pullman is the only character in his own book who never actually has to change,
right? Which is it's honestly the most brilliant subversive thing about the entire narrative.
Because he is a fixed point. Like August's face is the immovable object sitting right in the center of the room.
And every other character is just a variable bouncing off of him. Which I mean that fundamentally changes what we are doing here today.
It does because if you're listening to this, you probably think Wonder by R.J. Placio is, you know, a heartwarming story about a brave boy overcoming adversity, right?
The classic hero's journey, right? But I want you to completely forget that framing. Just wipe it from your mind.

Because this book is not a hero's journey for August. It is a psychological test. Oh, it is a brutal test. It really is. is a rigorous brutal test that you, the reader, and every single narrator in the
book is forced to take. What we are really analyzing is a social centrifuge.
You have one fixed unchangeable fact, which is August's severe facial difference, and around it this massive constellation of shifting And his reality truly is static.
I mean, by the time he's 10 years old, he has endured 27 surgeries. 27, right? Just incredible, right?
He has these medical mysteries, genetic anomalies that doctors can't even fully explain or like categorize.
The Natalie Merchant song that opens his section of the book says it perfectly. No, I love that part. Doctors stand over his bed disbelieving what they are seeing. He is the literal wonder.
Yeah. But the dramatic tension of the book, the engine that actually drives the plot forward, it doesn't come from August changing his face or even really changing his personality. No, not at all.
The tension comes entirely from how the world reacts to his face. Exactly.

So, let's look at the baseline facts before this test really kicks off. August is 10. He has been homeschooled his entire life by his mom, Isabelle, And she used to be a children's book illustrator, which is a great

little detail because she draws these beautiful fairies, but August notes that her her boy stuff isn't exactly great. Like, she once drew a Darth Vader that ended up looking like a weird mushroom-shaped That
is such a perfectly human detail. It is. And then you have his dad Nate and his older sister Via and they form this
incredibly tight just fiercely protective failins around him. But that intense protective orbit, I mean it didn't just organically develop over time.
it was forged in an absolute crucible the literal second he was born.
We really have to look at the birth We do because it perfectly encapsulates the dynamic of this family and well and the world at large.
The birth story is one of the most masterful pieces of writing in the book because of how it blends sheer trauma with dark absurd
Oh yeah. Like when mom tells the story to the kids, they always end up laughing even though the events themselves are genuinely harrowing.
Right. Because you have the doctors realizing two months before birth that there are um what they call small like maybe a cleft pallet.
Exactly. But absolutely nothing prepares the medical staff for the actual delivery room. You have this intense juxtaposition of characters in that room. You have a sweet nurse and then you
have another nurse with very big arms who is seemingly oblivious to social norms. She just keeps farting. She does. She just keeps farting.
She brings ice chips and she farts. She checks the blood pressure and she farts. She never says, "Excuse me." It's so absurd.
And to make matters worse, the regular doctor isn't even there. They are stuck with this cranky, inexperienced young resident they nicknamed Doogie.
And then August is delivered and the room just goes dead silent. That silence is so heavy.
The sweet nurse rushes the baby out of the room immediately. Dad follows them, literally dropping and shattering the video camera in his panic.

Mom is hysterical, trying to get out of the hospital bed. And this farting nurse is using her massive arms to hold mom down, yelling at her to stay calm. They both start screaming for the doctor to do something.

And then they realize the doctor has fainted. Out cold on the floor. He is literally out cold. And the absurdity just peaks when the farting nurse starts kicking the unconscious doctor with her foot, screaming, you know, what kind of doctor are you?
Get And then, according to family lore, she lets out the loudest, smelliest fart in the history of farts, which mom swears is what actually woke the doctor up. It's hilarious on the surface.
Like, it really is. But when you strip away the comedy, what is actually happening in that room? Well, it's pure panic.
If you connect this to the bigger picture, this is the very first moment the world reacts to
With fainting, with shattered cameras, with utter chaos. The world fails the test immediately. Exactly. But then the sweet nurse later whispers to mom, "Everyone born of God overcometh the world."

And that same nurse held mom's hand the next day when she finally met August. Mom says she was prepared for the seeing of him, but all she noticed was how pretty his eyes And from that exact second, the family locks
arms. They build a fortress. But now he's 10, The surgeries have slowed down. He's And the catalyst for our
psychological test arrives. The parents make the agonizing decision to send him to fifth grade at Beecher Prep under the guidance of middle school principal Mr.
Tushman. Which brings us to the transition from the safety of the bubble to the unforgiving reality of the world. And nothing symbolizes this transition
and really the psychology of masking better than the astronaut helmet. Okay. Yes. Picture August in a park on a summer day. It is a blistering 100° So
hot. And he is wearing this heavy plastic astronaut helmet that covers his entire head.
It was a gift from his sister's friend Miranda. He wore that helmet everywhere for 2 years straight.
Winter, summer, the beach. He says he loved it. He felt safe inside it.
Now hold that image of the kid in the helmet and contrast it with the moment he first walks into Mr. Tushman's office at Beer Prep.
The helmet is gone. August is completely exposed. He meets three kids for the first time. Jack, Will, Julian, and Charlotte.

And immediately they do what August calls the look away thing. I hate the look away thing. It's so real though. Their eyes dart to his face and then they instinctively, frantically look anywhere else.
Let's break down the psychology of this for you. [snorts] That helmet was never just a physical shield for August. It was a psychological shield for the rest of the That is such a good point.
It protected everyone else from having to take the test of seeing his face and processing their own discomfort. When that helmet comes off,
it's not just August who's exposed. Everyone else's character is suddenly violently on Absolutely. The helmet allowed people to look at him and just see

a little kid playing pretend. They could smile at the right? He was just a kid in a costume. But without it, they have to confront the trauma of his physical appearance, which makes them confront their
own empathy, or lack thereof. But this leads us to a crucial, devastating detail in the book. Where did the helmet go?
Oh, this breaks my heart. Because for years, August thought he simply lost it.
But we find out later his dad hid it. His dad literally threw it away. August is shattered when he finds this out.
Dad confesses and his reasoning is, "I couldn't stand seeing that thing cover your face anymore."
He tells August he didn't think it was good for him to hide. This sparks such a profound debate about parenting protection
and like exposure therapy. Dad forces the removal of the And I have to say, I think dad is actually incredibly cruel in this Oh wow.

let him wear the helmet. I get that, but stealing it, throwing it in the garbage, and then lying to his son's face about it for years is a massive betrayal of
Okay, look, I see exactly why you feel that way. And on a purely empathetic level for a suffering child, you have a Thank you.

Sure. Parents are fallible, but the intention was survival.

But if you don't expose a wound to the air, it never heals. Dad's heart had to shift first. He had to stop mourning the quote unquote normal kid he thought he would have and fiercely accept
the reality of the kid he does have. Without dad throwing away that helmet, August never develops the thick skin required to survive beacher prep.
I hear your argument about ripping off the bandage. But I still think robbing a kid of their one safe space is reckless.
Yes. What if August hadn't adapted? What if throwing the helmet away just made him agorophobic? Dad took a massive gamble with his son's mental health.
But the gamble paid off because dad understood the assignment. Dad shifted his own heart to prepare August for the sorting mechanism of the real world.
He removed the barrier. Okay, fine. I will concede that the physical barrier had to go for the test to even begin. But let's look closely at how the adults actively manufacture that test. Mr.

Tushman, the principal, implements a very specific welcome plan. Right. Tushman orchestrates what he calls a welcoming committee. Weeks before school even starts, he calls in three fifth grade students, Jack, Julian, and

He genuinely thought it would teach these kids a thing or two about empathy, friendship, and loyalty.
Which brings up a massive philosophical friction in this story. The tension between arranged kindness by adults
and chosen kindness by kids. Yes, the adults are manufacturing a scenario. They are artificially forcing proximity.
But you cannot manufacture genuine connection. No, you really can't. Let's look at Jack Will. Jack is very honest in his own chapters.

It was an obligation. But then Jack's internal state actually shifts. He chooses the It stops being a chore and he lists four highly specific
reasons why. One, he says you just get used to his face eventually. Two, August is actually a really cool dude who whispers hilarious things in class.

He's so funny in class. Three, he's incredibly smart and lets Jack cheat off him sometimes. August even lies to a teacher to protect Jack when they get caught having the exact same wrong answers on a homework which is such

a bro move. Totally. And for the most poignant reason, Jack realizes that if he could line up all the guys in the fifth grade against a wall and choose anyone to hang out with, he would genuinely choose
It perfectly illustrates the evolution from a mandate to a choice. But wait, I'm going to push back on Tushman's methods here.
I think forcing 10-year-olds to be a welcoming committee is deeply manipulative. Yes.
Look at the psychology of a 10-year-old. He is taking children who do not have the emotional maturity, the life experience or the prefrontal cortex development to process profound
facial deformity. And he is thrusting them into a situation where they are expected to be perfect little ambassadors of empathy. He is setting them up to fail. But if we explain the mechanics
of what Tushman is actually doing, he is installing moral training wheels. I don't know if I agree with that. Hear me out.

Yes, it's arranged. Yes, it's a bit manipulative. But empathy doesn't always just magically bloom out of nowhere. Sometimes it has to be modeled and structured before it can be Think about it like scaffolding

on a building. You need the scaffolding to hold the structure up while it's being built. Once the building is strong enough, you take the scaffolding away. If Tushman doesn't force that initial interaction, Jack will never sits down with August.
The fear of pure judgment would completely override Jack's natural goodness. Tushman creates a sanctioned adult approved space for them to But it places an incredible unfair burden on Jack.
You're asking a child to do the emotional heavy lifting of an That is the nature of the test. The adults can only set up the laboratory.
The kids are the ones who have to run the experiment. Touchman is effectively saying, "I will put you in the room with this reality, but what you do in the room is up to you.
Jack chooses to stay in the room. He builds the building." Right up until the scaffolding
because Jack doesn't stay in the room forever, which brings us to the moment the test completely breaks him. Let's look at Jack Will and the betrayal. Oh, this is one of the most agonizing
sequences in the novel. It is so painful to read. Imagine the cafeteria. It is weeks after Halloween. Jack is sitting with Summer and

Two words. She just says, "Bleeding scream." And you can feel the bottom drop out of Jack's entire world in that moment.
You really can. His brain races back to Halloween morning. He remembers standing in home room surrounded by Julian and the popular kids.
They were saying awful, vile things about August. Jack remembers chiming in. He remembers saying that if he looked like August,

He has armor for Right. He expects that from Julia. Exactly. But Jack was his safe harbor. Jack was the one who chose him when he didn't have to anymore.

That doesn't just hurt August's feelings. It shatters his entire framework of And there is a second detail from Jack's own perspective that makes his character even more complex.
Oh, right. Jack confesses to the reader that on the very first day of school, he actively avoided sitting with August in the Even though they had been in classes together all morning,

enjoying August's humor and copying his homework in private, but throwing him to the wolves the second it benefited his social standing.

this book doesn't grade on a curve based on age or evolutionary biology. The impact on August is exactly the same whether Jack is 10 or 30.

To Jack, it's juvenile stuff like, "You stink, big cheese." But to August, the notes are vicious, targeted hate speech.
Freak! Get out of our school, Orc. This type of warfare is insidious precisely because it thrives in the blind spots of the adults.

You're so pretty, Julian. I love you. Will you marry me? Love, Bula. It's brilliant. It really is. It shows they aren't just passive victims waiting for a savior.

treat him like a dirty secret, it is a terrible, selfish betrayal. I completely vehemently disagree with Really?

the plague. Or as August figures it out, it's exactly like the cheese touch from the book Diarrhea of a Wimpy Kid.
